introduction: With this evening Mass of the Lord's Supper, the Easter Triduum begins. We remember the night on which Jesus gave us the Eucharist, and the Church also remembers the gift of the priesthood. In the Gospel, the Lord washes his disciples' feet and gives us an example to follow. After Communion, the Blessed Sacrament is carried to a place of repose, and we are invited to stay and watch with him. Let us enter these holy days with grateful hearts.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, on this night Jesus loved his own to the end. Let us bring our prayers to the Father, through him.
intentions: For the Church, gathered around the table of the Lord: that the Eucharist may make her one body, serving the world in love. Let us pray to the Lord.
For bishops, priests and deacons: that they may serve God's people with the humility of Christ, who washed his disciples' feet. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are hungry, homeless or forgotten: that Christians may serve them as Jesus served, and share their bread with them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who will be received into the Church at Easter: that they may come with joy to the table of the Lord. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may watch and pray with Jesus tonight, and learn to wash one another's feet. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord Jesus, on the night before you suffered you gave us your Body and Blood and the example of your love. Teach us to receive you with faith and to serve one another as you have served us. You live and reign for ever and ever.

reflection.title: He loved them to the end
reflection.body:
The Triduum begins with a meal. The first reading recalls the first Passover in Egypt: a lamb without blemish, its blood on the doorposts, eaten in haste by people ready for a journey. God calls it "the LORD's Passover." He was about to set his people free.

Paul then hands on what he himself received: "that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread." Jesus said, "This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me." And Paul adds: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." Every Mass carries us back to this night.

John's Gospel does not describe the bread and the cup. Instead, it shows us what they mean. Jesus knows that his hour has come, and John writes: "having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end." Jesus gets up from the table, wraps a towel around his waist, and washes his disciples' feet, the work of a servant. Peter protests, but Jesus answers, "If I don't wash you, you have no part with me." Then he explains: "For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you."

The Eucharist and the washing of feet belong together. We cannot receive the Body of Christ and refuse to serve the members of his body. The psalm asks the right question: what can we give back to the Lord for all he has done? And it answers: "I will take the cup of salvation, and call on the LORD's name."

At the end of this Mass there is no blessing and no dismissal. The altar is stripped, and the Blessed Sacrament is taken to a place of repose. If you can, stay a little while tonight in silence before the Lord. He asked his friends to watch with him. Give him that time, and ask him whose feet he wants you to wash this year.
